# AI brainrot

Absurdist AI 3D: glossy hybrid creatures made of an object, an animal and sometimes a
food, introduced by a narrator who treats their nonsense lore as sacred history. The
register is loud, fast and completely sincere about something meaningless.

Invent originals with a chantable name and one signature prop or pose; never reuse the
viral named characters or anyone's mascot. The product can be a part. Chants and names
can use an invented, sing-song rhythm; keep it clearly made-up, never an imitation of a
real language or accent.

## Making it

**Gate it first.** Before any generation, confirm three things with the user as one
intake item:

- **Who approves:** someone who owns the brand voice, not just the requester.
- **Audience age:** the format is popular with children. If the audience skews under
  13, or the category is finance, health, alcohol or otherwise regulated, recommend
  another style.
- **What's off-limits:** competitors, real people, news events, violence, weapons,
  gross-out. Write the list into the style sheet.

Speed beats polish: make it while the trend is alive. Use `make-image` for each
character sheet (front, side, hero pose on a plain background), then animate from that
sheet with `make-ai-video` so the character stays consistent. Cast the narrator with
`voiceover` and audition over-the-top, dramatic reads. Build captions, name cards and
fake stats in `make-motion-graphics`. Plan a series: keep a lore sheet of names,
powers and rivalries so episodes build on each other.

**Keep out of prompts:** names of viral characters, real people, brands you don't own,
franchise names, realistic, gritty, gore, weapon, any real nationality or ethnicity.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Lukewarm or unreadable.** A narrator who hedges; a hybrid with too many parts. Commit.
- **Brand lost.** Put the product in the lore, not only in the end card.

# Claymation

Plasticine characters and props, nudged and shot one frame at a time.

Keep a faint surface boil, fingerprints and highlights shifting even on a held character; that flicker is the signature. Mouths snap between shapes, never morph. Titles are made in-world: clay letters, a hand-lettered card on a stand, a sticker on a clay laptop.

## Making it

Build the hero frame with `make-image`, then animate from it with `make-ai-video`. Generators give smooth motion, so retime every clip: resample to 12 fps with frame holds, deliver at 24, and leave fast gestures on ones. If a held shot is dead still, a light frame-to-frame texture jitter restores the boil. Author titles, captions and product text with `make-motion-graphics`, stepped on the same twos. Use `edit-in-blender` with clay shading and the same stepped timing when a character must repeat exact actions across many shots.

**Keep out of prompts:** 3D render, CGI, glossy, photoreal, motion blur, smooth animation, subsurface skin, hyperdetailed, vinyl toy.

## Working in a style

**When a style sheet is requested or needed for uncertain multi-shot consistency,**
keep it in the project. Translate it into each model's prompt syntax rather than pasting one paragraph everywhere:
see make-ai-video's [model prompting](../../make-ai-video/references/model-prompting.md)
and [audio and image prompting](../../choose-media-model/references/audio-image-prompting.md).
With an active design direction the style sheet is a summary of it; adopting saves the
accepted sheet via [design direction](../../brand-kit/references/directions.md).

**Hero frame and motion test, always early.** For a composed or styled video, make
a single hero frame in the style showing the real subject (the product, mascot or
office, not a generic example), then one 2–4 s moving test at the intended frame
rate and pacing, within the first few minutes. Present each as it exists with
`voyager files present PATH --deliverable none --json` with a one-line progress note that does not embed it (chat shows each as a card),
and keep building the rest without waiting for a reply.

**Hold consistency from the hero frame.** Derive later shots from the accepted frame
and character references instead of re-describing the style from scratch each time.

**Author exact things.** Words, logos, UI, numbers and dialogue boxes are built in
the motion or editing tool over generated imagery.

**Keep the user's tool.** Style guides use the motion skill's default tool unless
a look needs another. A motion tool the user named in this
conversation, or else a saved one, still comes first.

**Evoke an era or a medium, not an owner.** Don't name living artists, studios,
directors, franchises or games in prompts or on screen, and don't reproduce
trademarked characters, logos or signature UI.

# Dark keynote

The launch-film look for software: a near-black stage, a hairline grid, cool soft light, a single brand accent, and interface pieces that move with snap-to-grid exactness. No hardware appears; the interface is the hero: a cursor, a window, a notification, a wall of tiles, one enormous number. Tension comes from contrast: clutter generated by rule, a single decisive action, then open space.

- Draw every component in code and invent it (for a real product, use its real screens or rebuild them from its screenshots): nothing borrowed from a real OS (no coloured window buttons, menu bar or dock).
- A single accent, saturated and glowing, belongs to the product alone: its hero element, call to action, confirmations and headline number. Two things in accent means one is a mistake.
- One living element may perform. Exits are designed (retracting a part per beat, a CRT-style squash to a point); nothing simply fades.
- Make the score an audible process: two voices phasing, a note added each bar, notes stripped until one remains, or one chord everything resolves onto. Two sound families carry the plot. Clutter sounds scattered: detuned, panned at random, every source a different timbre. The product is one family: felt ticks and glass taps in a single mode, dead centre.

## Making it

Author it in `make-motion-graphics`: the UI kit, the 2.5D camera, typed spawns, curved flights and the light reveal all live in code, and the rule-generated disorder needs state. Generate elements by rule and pad or trim the result to the exact slot count so no grid ever has a hole. Use `edit-in-blender` only if a device must appear, rendered dark with the same single accent. Make the process score in `make-sound` and time picture events to its beats; make the two foley families there too. Generated video has no role; a real product screen can come in through `screen-capture` and be restyled.

**Keep out of prompts (reference stills only):** glass render, physical product, scanlines, warm tones, gradients everywhere.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Flicker, not collapse.** Elements snapping to the nearest slot. Give each a typed destination, a curve and a trail.

# Doodle over footage

Hand-drawn scribbles, arrows, circles, faces, speech bubbles and scrawled notes animated on top of real video, as if someone drew on the footage with a marker. The register is casual, funny and personal: it adds commentary, emphasis and inner thoughts to footage that would otherwise be plain.

Drawings stick to what they annotate: track the subject so the doodle moves, scales and turns with it, then wobbles on top.

## Making it

Find the moments first with `edit-video` (the laugh, the reveal, the line worth underlining) and cut the edit before drawing. Build overlays through `make-motion-graphics` for locked-off shots, screen recordings and hand-keyed follows. Doodles that track moving subjects go in `edit-in-after-effects` when the user names it; otherwise anchor per-frame boxes (locate-and-safe-areas) in `make-motion-graphics`, or keep doodles on locked-off moments. Generate drawn elements with `make-image` as line art on plain white or black, then key or blend them over the footage, making two or three variants of each drawing to cycle as the boiling line. Author handwritten words rather than generating them. Posterize overlay timing to 8 to 12 fps while footage plays at full rate.

Keep out of prompts: vector, clean line art, gradient, 3D, realistic, shading, logo, photographic background.

## Where it goes wrong

- Jokes at the expense of people on camera; keep annotations affectionate and confirm consent for faces.

# Felt stop-motion

Needle-felted wool, knitted yarn and fabric characters moved frame by frame through small, cozy sets. It is softer and quieter than clay.

Movement is small and slow: breathing, blinking, a weight shift, a nudged cup. A settle is one soft extra pose, never a bounce.

## Making it

Make the hero frame with `make-image`, plus a character reference sheet for recurring puppets, then animate from it with `make-ai-video`. Keep prompted actions small. Retime every clip: resample to 12 fps with frame holds, deliver at 24, and stretch holds on quiet beats. Author labels, captions and product names with `make-motion-graphics`, stepped to the same timing. Use `edit-in-blender` with fiber shading only when staging must be precise and repeatable.

**Keep out of prompts:** plush toy, fleece, 3D render, CGI, glossy, smooth, vibrant, neon, realistic fur.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Real fur.** Animals grow photoreal hair. Push felted-wool wording and choose flatter takes.

# Frutiger Aero

The glossy optimism of early-2000s consumer tech: aqua gradients, glass buttons,
bubbles, droplets, green hills under blue skies and a lens flare.

Invent the UI chrome; never use a real operating system's logo, wallpaper or window
design.

## Making it

Generate environments and material shots with `make-image` and animate them with
`make-ai-video`: hills, skies, underwater scenes, droplets and bubbles are where
generation shines. Build windows, buttons, text, logos and data cards in
`make-motion-graphics` with real gradients, highlights and
reflections. Use `edit-in-blender` when a glossy product
or orb needs precise, repeatable reflections. The signature quality generators miss
is the specular gloss: add highlight bands, glints and bloom in the authored layer.

Keep out of prompts: vaporwave, synthwave, neon, dark mode, grunge, cyberpunk,
purple and pink sunset, flat design, matte.

## Where it goes wrong

- Real OS logos, wallpapers or window chrome slipping in from generated images. Repaint.

# Hologram HUD

A product scanned into a glowing line drawing floating over a projector disc against a near-black stage. Brackets snap onto its parts in turn, each slides open to show its insides, a leader runs out to a card, and the card's number settles from scrambled glyphs into its true value. It reads as live data computed in front of the viewer.

Build real topology: every part touches another; the eye finds a floating piece first. Time to the music: one bar carries one fact. Density tracks information: half-time under reading, a single beat of absolute digital silence, a drop for the biggest change.

## Making it

Build the wireframe scene in `edit-in-blender`: model the object from real parts with assembly axes, render edges as additive lines with depth fog and glow, and drive the camera, scan plane and explodes from a timeline keyed to the music's bars. Author the HUD (plates, target boxes, leaders, rolling values, chip rail, subtitles) in `make-motion-graphics` so numbers come from data and lock on exact frames, and composite it sharp over the 3D render; a HUD-only loop screen can carry a 2D wireframe there too. A simple object can be extruded from a 2D path instead of modelled. Make the arpeggio bed in `make-sound` at a tempo where one bar carries one fact, and the lock, roll and servo sounds there too. Generated video cannot hold a wireframe or a number; use it for nothing here.

**Keep out of prompts (reference stills only):** rendered product, glossy, lens flare, scanlines.

# Ink wash

Brush painting in the East Asian tradition, set in motion: five tones of black ink over warm rice paper, most of every frame left bare, one red for the seal. Scenes are painted into being, not cut to.

Bare paper is substance, not background. If the brand colour is not red, the seal still carries the mark in red and the brand colour stays off screen. A decisive stroke should arrive out of silence rather than on a beat. Keep the voice calm and rare, like a colophon that never explains the painting.

## Making it

Author strokes in `make-motion-graphics`: each stroke a path carrying pressure, wetness and bristle breaks, seeded from its own index and evaluated along normalised arc length so the white gaps hold still; washes as a noisy radial mask with a tide-line; the paper as one fixed layer. Paint hero frames and the handscroll plate in `make-design`, or generate plates with `make-image` prompted monochrome and mostly empty, then split them into layers for the pan and add only ripples, mist and a bloom with `make-ai-video` from a locked camera; a generator cannot keep stroke order, so it must never paint the strokes themselves. Make the zither cues in `make-sound` to the picture, and the drop, brush and seal sounds there too.

**Keep out of prompts:** watercolour colour, outlines, vector, flat fill, photoreal, anime, calligraphy title.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Vector brush.** A closed outline with brush texture pasted inside. Let the stroke be the form.

# Isometric infographic

A diagram you can walk around: flat three-tone blocks in true isometric on a floating board, hairline ink leaders, pinned labels and quantities counted in repeated icons. Walls slide away to show what is inside, a drawn route pulls the eye through, and a final pull-back leaves a finished infographic on screen.

Hue is meaning, as in a legend: each material or role owns a hue and none share. A line always leads: the route draws a little ahead of what follows it, a leader grows before its inset opens, and the cut mark is drawn before the wall moves. Solids enter by moving, never by alpha; a translucent block looks like a ghost.

## Making it

Author it in `make-motion-graphics`, generating the scene from data (counts, routes, stations) with a depth-sorted draw queue when it needs one. Write the projection and three-tone shading once and derive every face from it; cull small world detail past a zoom threshold and tie tall objects' opacity to zoom so a pull-back never drags a huge shape across the frame. Use `edit-in-blender` only when the board must be a real model with many repeatable views, rendered orthographic with flat shading. Make the bed in `make-sound` and land icon fills on its subdivisions, with its foley. Image generation only for concept frames; generated "isometric" art mixes projections and must not be cut in.

**Keep out of prompts (concept frames only):** perspective, lighting, shadows, texture, low-poly, 3D render, outlines.

# Low-poly life-sim

Chunky early-3D people living small office lives, seen through the interface of a
life-simulation game. Ordinary work becomes a managed routine: needs drain, a menu
offers "Refill coffee", the character answers in gibberish.

**The overlay is half the style.** Need bars are labeled with invented needs
("Focus", "Caffeine", "Inbox"), a radial pie menu pops from a clicked object, and
speech bubbles show pictograms (coffee cup, bug, chart), never words. Characters move
with game logic, not acting; nothing lands on a musical beat, only on a click.

## Making it

Use `edit-in-blender` for true low-poly: flat shading, small textures, a
fixed overhead camera, keyframed canned loops. `make-ai-video` drifts toward smooth
modern 3D; use it only for background lots or tests from an accepted `make-image`
hero frame. Build every overlay in `make-motion-graphics`
and composite it so meters, menus and pictograms stay exact. Record gibberish with
`voiceover` from written nonsense syllables, auditioned first.

Keep out of prompts: realistic, cinematic, animated-feature style, subsurface, depth
of field, ray-traced, highly detailed, 8K.

## Where it goes wrong

- Words in speech bubbles, or meters that move without a visible cause.
- Gibberish that sounds like a real language, or one clip on repeat.

# Midcentury cartoon

Limited animation in the flat 1950s manner: colour fills sitting a few pixels off a thin ink line that breathes, geometric people who hold still from the shoulders down while their hands work, rooms reduced to a colour plane and a floor band, a narrator with classroom calm and a cool-jazz trio. The style does a job (set-up guides, how-tos, safety cards, onboarding flows) instead of telling a story, and the viewer should finish knowing how to do the thing.

- The presenter is one held drawing; only arms and hands, eyes and mouth move. The product alone wears its brand colour.
- Transitions are iris circles, solid-colour wipes and cuts on the beat; dissolves are banned.
- On the beat before the key action, cut every sound including room tone, so the first thing heard after (a click, a pour) is the step itself.

## Making it

Author it in `make-motion-graphics`: cards, call-outs, medallions and wipes with the cel offset as a per-fill transform re-rolled on twos, and the presenter's pose switching, kneel rig and data-driven steps. Draw characters and props as line and fill layers so the fills can misregister. Design the character sheet, the card system and any printed companion in `make-design` with the same palette, and animate from those files. `make-image` can supply reference and flat props prompted as 1950s flat illustration, reduced to the palette by hand; `make-ai-video` cannot keep a body still or a fill registered, so leave it out. Make the combo in `make-sound` with a chord change per step, and the stamp, click and swish sounds there too.

**Keep out of prompts:** 3D, gradient, outlines closed, rubber hose, anime, photoreal, modern flat corporate.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Steps that don't land.** A hand action falling between beats. End every action on a beat with its data arriving at the same instant.

# Painted anime

Hand-painted environments with simple cel-shaded characters, used for quiet, cinematic slice-of-life moments: a train window at golden hour, a convenience store glowing at dusk, rain on a side street, steam off a bowl of noodles. The register is nostalgic, tender and a little wistful; ordinary routines feel meaningful.

Design characters as originals from the brand's audience; avoid signature hairstyles, outfits, creatures or faces from existing work. Most movement isn't the character: slow pans across a painting, parallax between foreground, midground and sky, drifting clouds, wind in hair and fabric, rain, curling steam.

## Making it

Generate background plates with `make-image`, wide enough for any pan. Generate characters separately on simple backgrounds from a reference sheet so they stay consistent. Add subtle life to plates (clouds, steam, rain) with `make-ai-video` image-to-video, prompting minimal motion and a locked camera. Build parallax pans and composites in `make-motion-graphics` by splitting paintings into layers. For limited-animation timing, hold the character layer at 8 or 12 fps over the smooth background instead of keeping the generator's fluid motion.

Keep out of prompts: 3D render, photorealistic, glossy, chibi, action pose, speed lines, neon cyberpunk, heavy black outlines.

# Paper cutout

Flat pieces of paper and card, cut out, jointed and moved like puppets on a lit tabletop. Played cute, it suits education, nonprofits, children's products and friendly explainers; built as collage from found imagery, it turns absurdist and satirical.

Keep puppets in profile or three-quarter view; flat pieces can't turn. A piece that grows or shrinks is scaled whole, never redrawn at a new size, or its cut edge shimmers.

## Making it

Build the hero frame with `make-image`. For puppets, generate each character and prop as separate flat pieces on plain backgrounds so they can be cut out and rigged. Assemble and animate in `make-motion-graphics`: pinned joints, stepped rotation, replacement faces, multiplane parallax and authored drop shadows. Use `make-ai-video` only for loose atmospheric shots, resampled to 12 fps with holds and delivered at 24.

**Keep out of prompts:** 3D, vector illustration, flat design, clean edges, gradient, glossy, isometric, CGI, digital painting.

## Where it goes wrong

- **No gap shadows.** Layers without shadows collapse into one printed image; every layer casting the same shadow flattens the stack just as much.

# Pastel storybook

A dollhouse view of ordinary life: dead-centered, symmetrical frames in dusty pastels,
people facing the lens with straight faces, and the day divided into chapters. The
register is dry and quietly affectionate; mundane office rituals get the gravity of a
fable. It is a proven short-form format for "a day at our company", shot on a phone.

Hold a static frame a half-second longer than feels natural so the deadpan lands, then
cut hard to a title card. Almost centered reads as a mistake.

## Making it

Real footage is the main route. On a phone: tripod or flat surface, 1x lens and step
back (the ultrawide bends verticals), grid and level on, exposure and focus locked,
subject on the center line at chest height. Choose backgrounds that are already
symmetrical: doorways, corridors, shelving. Fake a dolly by sliding the phone along a
table edge or pushing a rolling chair steadily. For vertical delivery, stack the
symmetry in a doorway or tall shelf.

Use `edit-video` to find centered, level moments in existing footage. Build chapter and name cards in
`make-motion-graphics`. Use `make-image` and
`make-ai-video` for exteriors or a miniature facade the crew can't shoot; generators
default to off-center, shallow-focus, moody frames, so ask for the opposite.

**Keep out of prompts:** cinematic, moody, bokeh, shallow
depth of field, dynamic angle, dramatic lighting, handheld, neon, teal and orange.

# 16-bit pixel RPG

The company's world as a 16-bit console role-playing game: small sprite heroes,
tiled maps, a dialogue box typing one line at a time, a jingle when a quest is
accepted.

**One pixel grid.** Choose a native canvas (320x180 for 16:9, 180x320 vertical) and
draw everything on it: sprites, tiles, UI and text. Upscale by a whole number with
nearest-neighbor sampling. No mixed pixel sizes, rotation, free scaling,
anti-aliasing or blur. Everything snaps to whole pixels; use a bitmap pixel font on
the grid, never a scaled vector font. Dither only skies, glows and gradients, with an
ordered pattern anchored to its layer so it moves with that layer instead of swimming
as the camera scrolls. Big pose changes get one in-between drawing; at these frame
rates a single jump between poses reads as a glitch.

## Making it

Author the finished animation in `make-motion-graphics` at
native resolution, upscaled by nearest-neighbor at render, so the grid, palette,
typewriter text and positions are exact. Use `make-image` for concept frames,
portraits and tile sheets, then reduce them to the palette, resample to native size
by nearest-neighbor and fix stray pixels and outlines by eye. `make-ai-video` does
not hold a pixel grid; use it for reference only.

Keep out of prompts: HD, realistic, smooth shading, soft glow, depth of field, 3D
render, voxel, painterly.

## Where it goes wrong

- Mixed pixel sizes, such as a sprite scaled by 1.5 or text on a finer grid. The one exception is a 2x
  punch-in, where the whole scene doubles and the dialogue box and UI stay at their
  normal size on top.
- Dialogue boxes crammed with text, or closed as soon as typing ends. Keep lines
  short and readable at phone size.
- Three or more near-black frames in the middle of a block or dither wipe. It reads
  as the viewer blinking; start revealing the next shot as soon as the last one is
  covered. A uniform one-pixel dither across the whole frame reads as a screen door;
  dissolve as an expanding ring instead.

# Printmaking

Animation that looks pulled from a press, frame by frame: a few inks on paper, plates a little off each other, transitions from the print shop. Three sub-registers share one grammar: **risograph** (a few translucent spot inks on warm paper, cheap, bright, zine-like), **woodcut** (black ink where every light area is a knife cut, heavy, emotional, wordless) and **copperplate engraving** (tone from swelling, tapering lines, exact and learned).

Every plate sits a few pixels off its neighbours; text is printed too, so it misregisters and grains with its plate; the paper margin never moves. Never re-roll registration per frame. Nothing printed ever fades. In engraving a constant-width line is a vector drawing and never belongs. Put characters on twos at 12 fps and everything else (camera, light, fire, liquid) on ones at 24; a stepped camera judders.

## Making it

Author it in `make-motion-graphics`: draw each frame as plates (one channel per ink, so overprint and knockout are exact), then "print" it in a shader pass with per-plate offset and rotation, halftone on a rotated grid fixed to the paper rather than to objects, grain, pinholes and streaks. Carve reveals and swelling burin strokes are stroke lists with their own timings. Design posters, the zine pages and the engraved plate itself in `make-design` with the same ink set, then animate from those files. Use `make-image` for reference and for a photo to be re-cut as a woodcut or engraving, reduced to the plate logic by hand; never drop generated "riso" or "woodcut" art straight in; it carries hundreds of colours and no plates. Make the music in `make-sound`, and the press, knife and burin sounds there too.

**Keep out of prompts:** vector, gradient, glossy, photoreal, outline, CMYK pop art, screen print.

# Puffy 3D

Soft, inflatable objects like vinyl balloons, pool toys or squeezed marshmallows, set on clean studio backdrops and animated with a satisfying bounce and jiggle. The register is friendly, tactile and premium at once. It suits simple, iconic subjects: a logo, an app icon, a product silhouette, a few UI symbols.

Thin parts vanish when inflated, so thicken strokes and close counters.

## Making it

Use `edit-in-blender` when the logo or type must be exact, objects collide, or the jiggle must be controlled: import the SVG, extrude, remesh, inflate with Blender cloth pressure or soft body, then bake drops and collisions. For props and atmosphere, `make-image` hero frames animated with `make-ai-video` work, but generators under-deliver jiggle: prompt the physical action ("drops, squashes, bounces twice and settles") and reject takes that float or stay rigid. Add exact supporting type in `make-motion-graphics`.

Keep out of prompts: chrome, glossy plastic, glass, metallic, hyperrealistic, clay, fur, cartoon outline, cluttered background, sharp bevel.

## Where it goes wrong

- Hard shapes with a glossy coat instead of pillowed edges and visible seams.

# Retro desktop

The whole story plays on a late-1990s or early-2000s computer screen: a cursor
hesitates, an error popup interrupts, a chat window blinks, a progress bar stalls at
99%.

Invent the OS: its own name, start button, taskbar clock and icons. Never reproduce a
real vendor's logo, wallpaper or exact window design. The cursor is the camera and the
actor. Use original sounds in the era's spirit, not famous recorded OS sounds.

## Making it

Build it almost entirely as authored UI in `make-motion-graphics`. Draw the chrome as
vector shapes and text, and keyframe the cursor path by hand. Use `make-image` only for wallpapers,
photos inside windows and icon concepts, then reduce them to a small palette.
`screen-capture` suits a real modern product appearing inside the fake desktop.
Keep `make-ai-video` for rare off-screen cutaways, like a hand on a beige mouse.

Keep out of prompts: modern flat UI, glassmorphism, dark mode, high resolution,
vaporwave.

## Where it goes wrong

- Chrome that is too modern: rounded corners, smooth icons, a modern font.
- Text too small at phone size. Crop into the active window and let the cursor lead.

# Rubber hose cartoon

Early-1930s theatrical cartoons: boneless, bendy characters with pie-cut eyes and white gloves in a world where everything bounces to the beat, printed on scratchy black-and-white or faded early-color film. The register is charming, musical and slightly unhinged: surreal gags, objects that come alive and sing.

Design originals, not the famous mice, cats, sailors or flappers, nor anything from modern games that revived the look. Everything dances: idle characters bob on every beat, trees sway in rhythm; choose the music first.

## Making it

Design characters with `make-image` first and lock a turnaround sheet. `make-ai-video` can animate short dances and gags from accepted frames, but generators drift toward smooth modern motion and color: prompt rhythmic bouncing on the beat and reject takes that lose the line style. Build title cards, iris wipes, exact lettering and the film surface (grain, scratches, flicker, weave, vignette) in `make-motion-graphics`.

Keep out of prompts: 3D, glossy, anime, realistic anatomy, modern color grading, sharp digital lines.

## Where it goes wrong

- Clean digital line with grain pasted on top; the line wobble and the film surface must agree.
- Period stereotypes slipping in through generated crowds or gags; remove them.

# Silent film

A one-reeler from the 1920s shown as a picture house would have shown it: a 4:3 print inside a gate, theatre curtains either side, silver tones that flicker and weave, scratches and burns creeping in from the edges, intertitle cards in place of dialogue, a pianist scoring every beat live. No one talks; bodies act in wide shots and the cards cover the rest.

- No bowler-and-cane pastiche. At most one element keeps its real colour through the print, and only when it is what the film is about.
- A card never repeats what is already on screen.
- Sample like a hand crank: figures and camera at 16 fps while the damage layer (flicker, weave, grain, scratches) refreshes on every output frame at 24. That mismatch reads as projection rather than a low frame rate.
- The pianist follows the picture, never the reverse.

## Making it

Build the picture in `make-motion-graphics`, keyframing figures and the chain and running the print pass as a shader. Keep the print pass as one stackable layer (tone, flicker, weave, scratches, burn, grain, dust) applied over everything, with a colour mask for the one kept colour. Use `make-image` and `make-ai-video` for scenes, prompted monochrome and wide, then run them through the same ink and print pass so they match; redraw the company's real footage the same way. Design intertitle cards and the poster in `make-design` with the deco border system. Make the score in `make-sound` with its cues keyed to the picture; add the projector there too.

**Keep out of prompts:** colour, modern haircuts, lens flare, HDR, smooth video, bowler hat and cane.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Mannequin close-ups.** A big close-up of a rigged or generated face looks dead. Keep faces small, or frame them inside an iris.
- **Sepia filter.** Smooth modern animation under a brown tint. Drawing and sampling must be period too.

# Swiss motion

Mid-century typographic poster design, animated: a modular grid, a single typeface, black type and bars on paper, one hot signal colour, moves timed like a press stroke. Nothing drifts; each element locks to the grid and each arrival hits a beat, so whichever element refuses the system reads as a character.

One element wears the signal colour at any moment and that element is the lead. Subtitles live inside the layout at the head of a column, never in a bottom strip. Skip the two famous mid-century grotesques; use an open-licence neo-grotesque. Enter by wipe or clip-reveal, never fade. The rule-breaker alone moves linear, off-grid, and may stall mid-move.

## Making it

Author everything in `make-motion-graphics`. Define the grid, the curves and the tempo in code once, and derive every position and duration from them; land each visual onset on a whole frame so beats don't flicker. Make the pulse in `make-sound` first, at a tempo whose subdivisions give usable snap durations, and cut to its grid; foley there too. Generation has no role here except reference imagery.

**Keep out of prompts (reference stills only):** gradient, glow, 3D, grain, kinetic typography, Bauhaus primary shapes.

# Tilt-shift miniature

A real place or product made to look like a tiny model: a toy-town office, a factory on a tabletop, a city block like a railway layout. The effect comes from a thin band of focus, a high vantage and busy, stepped little movements.

## Making it

**Real footage made miniature.** Use high, wide, locked-off or slow footage the company has or can shoot. In post, add a graded focus-band blur, lift saturation and contrast, speed it up and step the frame rate, in `make-motion-graphics` or an ffmpeg recipe (`edit-in-after-effects` when the user names it). Low or shallow-focus footage won't convert well; say so. **Built or generated diorama.** Make the hero frame with `make-image` as a physical model, animate small actions with `make-ai-video`, then apply the same speed-up and stepping. Use `edit-in-blender` when the set must be precise or reused, rendering a real narrow depth of field. Author signs, labels and numbers as overlays.

**Keep out of prompts:** eye level, close-up, cinematic, moody, overcast, fog, portrait bokeh, dramatic lighting, handheld.

## Where it goes wrong

- **Faces up close.** Recognizable faces break scale and raise consent issues. Keep people small.

# Whiteboard explainer

A marker drawing on a white board, built line by line while a cartoon hand follows the pen tip and a narrator explains.

Everything arrives by being drawn; nothing pops in. The hand holds the marker at the pen tip and covers the area below and right of it, so lay each board out from top-left toward the centre and draw in reading order. Characters act after the hand leaves. Give each accent colour a job (red for the problem, green for the fix, the brand color for the product).

## Making it

Write and record the narration first, then plan the board against it: where each idea is drawn, and which word cues each drawing, so every drawing lands on the line that names it. Script and cue-sheet rules are in [narrated explainers](../../make-motion-graphics/references/narrated-explainer.md).

Generate icons, characters and props with `make-image` as clean black line art on plain white, one element per image, then reduce each to centerlines and draw them on in `make-motion-graphics` with the stroke-ordering and draw-on method in [illustrative motion](../../make-motion-graphics/references/illustrative-motion.md). Use monoline strokes at the board's one width rather than tapered ink. Author handwritten text as draw-on paths in a handwriting face. Put the hand on its own layer: one generated or traced hand-with-marker image, positioned each frame at the current pen tip, with the marker cap tinted to the ink being drawn. `make-ai-video` can't hold a line weight or draw in order; don't use it for board shots.

**Keep out of prompts:** 3D, gradient, realistic, shading, texture, watercolor, vector illustration, isometric, colored background.

# Video styles

When the brief names or clearly describes one of the styles below, read its guide and
[working in a style](references/common.md) before the first frame. When the brief asks for
something stylized without choosing ("make it fun", "something handmade", "go viral"),
offer three styles from different groups that fit its subject and audience best, with
a recommendation, as one intake item. When the brief wants a look that isn't here,
proceed without these guides and don't mention them.

## Tactile and handmade

- [Claymation](references/claymation.md): chunky, thumbprinted characters and slightly jerky stop-motion. Warm and funny; mascots and product explainers.
- [Felt stop-motion](references/felt-stop-motion.md): needle-felted and knitted characters in cozy sets. Softer than clay; wellness, food and lifestyle.
- [Paper cutout](references/paper-cutout.md): flat paper pieces with visible edges, animated like puppets. Crafty-cute or absurdist.
- [Tilt-shift miniature](references/tilt-shift-miniature.md): a tiny toy-town version of a product, office or city.

## Retro-digital nostalgia

- [Low-poly life-sim](references/low-poly-life-sim.md): chunky early-3D with life-sim game overlays. "Day in the life of our PM."
- [16-bit pixel RPG](references/pixel-art-rpg.md): sprites, dialogue boxes and "Quest accepted!" moments. Onboarding, product tours, hiring.
- [Frutiger Aero](references/frutiger-aero.md): Y2K gloss, bubbles, glass and aqua gradients from the early-2000s desktop.
- [Retro desktop](references/retro-desktop.md): the story plays out in old OS windows, error popups, cursors and chat apps. Meme-native and cheap.

## Graphic and print

- [Swiss motion](references/swiss-motion.md): a modular grid, one typeface, one signal colour, snaps on the beat and knife cuts. Brand systems, manifestos, a number that matters.
- [Isometric infographic](references/isometric-infographic.md): a three-tone isometric diorama with cutaways, label pins and icon-built numbers. How-it-works and impact stories.
- [Printmaking](references/printmaking.md): risograph, woodcut and copperplate engraving as one family: limited inks, misregistration, paper. Editorial weight without gloss.
- [Ink wash](references/ink-wash.md): East Asian brush painting with empty paper, bleeding washes and one red seal. Craft, calm, parable.
- [Dark keynote](references/dark-keynote.md): the software launch look: near-black stage, hairline grid, one accent, UI that snaps on the beat. Launches and performance claims.
- [Hologram HUD](references/hologram-hud.md): an object scanned into a glowing wireframe with target locks, exploded parts and rolling numbers. Spec walkthroughs and teardowns.

## Illustrated and motion design

- [Puffy 3D](references/puffy-3d.md): soft, inflatable, balloon-like objects that bounce and jiggle.
- [Painted anime](references/painted-anime.md): watercolor backgrounds and cinematic slice-of-life moments.
- [Rubber hose cartoon](references/rubber-hose.md): 1930s bendy limbs and pie-eyes, black-and-white or faded color.
- [Midcentury cartoon](references/midcentury-cartoon.md): flat 1950s limited animation, geometric figures, off-register colour and a classroom narrator. Set-up guides, rules, onboarding.
- [Silent film](references/silent-film.md): a projected 1920s print with intertitles, an iris, film damage and a cinema pianist. Comedy of process and heritage.
- [Doodle over footage](references/doodle-over-footage.md): hand-drawn scribbles, arrows and faces animated on real video the company already has.
- [Whiteboard explainer](references/whiteboard-explainer.md): a marker drawing built line by line with a hand following the pen, under narration. Concept and process explainers.

## Meme-native

- [Pastel storybook](references/pastel-storybook.md): centered symmetrical framing, pastel palettes and deadpan title cards. "A day at our company."
- [AI brainrot](references/ai-brainrot.md): surreal hybrid characters, dramatic narration and nonsense lore. Highest ceiling, shortest shelf life.
